content:
Child marriage is a real problem in parts of the world, Muslim and non-Muslim, and it is often defended with religion. Campaigners and critics ask whether Islam permits it, and defenders sometimes answer by pointing to the example of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.

This article sets out what the Islamic sources say, kept apart from custom. It covers the Quran, the requirement of consent, the disagreement among the classical jurists, the reports about Aisha and what weight they carry, and the laws that Muslim-majority countries have passed since.

The Quran does not state a minimum age. It speaks of orphans who "reach the age of marriage" and tells guardians to test their sound judgement before handing over their property.[1] The verse links marriageable age with the ability to manage affairs, and the jurists drew on that link when they discussed maturity (bulūgh).

Marriage in the Quran's framework is a mīthāq ghalīẓ, a solemn covenant.[2] A covenant needs a party who can understand and agree to it. The phrase appears in the verse that reminds husbands of what they have taken from their wives, and it sets the seriousness of the bond high.

The objection is that a standard of understanding is not a number, and that societies have applied it loosely. That is correct. The Quran gives a test and leaves the application to the community, which is why the age at which a person is ready has been argued in every period.

The jurists distinguished two thresholds. Maturity (bulugh) was marked by the physical signs of adulthood or, failing them, by an age: fifteen for most of the schools, and seventeen or eighteen in the view attributed to Abu Hanifa.[3] Sound judgement (rushd), the capacity the verse on orphans asks guardians to test, was a separate question, and a person could reach the first without the second. The verse ties the handing over of property to both.[1] Many modern scholars argue that marriage, which hands over far more than property, should be held to the same standard.

The Prophet (peace be upon him) said that a previously married woman may not be married until she is consulted, and a virgin until her permission is asked.[4] The Companions asked how a virgin gives permission, and he answered that her silence is permission. The rule applies to the first marriage as much as to later ones.

When a woman told him that her father had married her to someone she disliked, he gave her the choice to refuse.[5] The report shows that a guardian's authority did not override the bride's own right to accept or decline.

The strongest objection is that the rule speaks of a woman who can be consulted, and says nothing about a child who cannot. The jurists faced the same difficulty, and it is why they differed over minors, as the next entry shows. The consent hadiths remain the clearest statement of the law and the standard against which any marriage is judged.

Ismail al Faruqi summarises the rule on a marriage arranged by parents for a minor: on reaching adulthood, the young person has the full right to confirm the contract or reject it, and may dissolve the marriage even if it has already been consummated.[6]

The case of Khansa bint Khidham shows the rule in practice. Her father married her to a man she did not want, and she went to the Prophet, who annulled the marriage.[7] In the Hanafi school, an adult woman may contract her own marriage without a guardian, which places the decision in the hands of the person whose life it shapes. The schools differ on the role of the guardian, and they agree that he may not marry an adult woman against her will.

Some jurists allowed a father to contract the marriage of a minor daughter, with consummation delayed until she is able. Others, among them early scholars such as Ibn Shubruma and Uthman al-Batti, held that a marriage before maturity is not valid.[8] The point is that the question was argued inside the tradition and not settled.

Those who allowed it relied on the reports about Aisha and on the Quran's mention of a waiting period for women who have not menstruated (65:4).[9] Those who refused it read the consent hadiths and the Quran's requirement of sound judgement as ruling out a contract made for a child, and some read the waiting-period verse as covering women whose cycles are delayed.

Even among those who permitted it, the permission came with conditions. Consummation waited until the girl was physically able, and the guardian had to act in her interest. The Hanafi school gave a girl married as a minor the option to end the marriage on reaching maturity. The tradition therefore never treated the matter as unrestricted.

The dissenting view has a clear classical record. The Hanafi jurist al-Sarakhsi reports that Ibn Shubruma and Abu Bakr al-Asamm held that no one may marry off a minor, boy or girl, until they reach maturity, arguing that the purpose of marriage cannot be served before then and that a guardian has no need to decide it on the child's behalf.[10] That view was a minority in the classical period. It is the view that many modern legislators in Muslim-majority countries have effectively adopted.

On consummation, the jurists were united that no fixed age made it lawful. Al-Nawawi, commenting on the reports about A'isha, wrote that it depends on the girl being physically able to bear it without harm, and that if she is not, the husband must wait however old she is.[11] The principle of no harm, which the jurists applied throughout family law, governs the question.

The best-known report concerns the Prophet's marriage to Aisha, which is discussed with the evidence in its own article on this site. Al-Bukhari records that she was six at the contract and nine at consummation.[12] Scholars distinguish between what the Prophet did as a particular case, in a society with different norms, and what he commanded as law. The commands on consent and maturity are the law.

The objection is that the Prophet's life is itself a source of law, so a report about his marriage carries legal weight. Scholars answer that his actions fall into several kinds. Some are general models, and others belong to his own circumstances. A marriage contracted in the society of seventh-century Arabia, where marriage at a young age was common and accepted, does not by itself make a rule for later societies.

Scholars also differ over the reports themselves. Some modern writers have questioned the ages given, pointing to the transmission of the report by Hisham ibn Urwa in Iraq and to other chronological clues; most hadith scholars accept the ages as reported. The evidence on both sides is set out in 5 questions about Aisha, answered from the sources. Whichever view a reader takes, the legal argument above does not depend on it.

Egypt, Turkey and Tunisia set 18 as the minimum age, and Morocco did so with a court exception. Muslim jurists have defended such laws as in keeping with the purposes of sharia (maqāṣid), which include protecting a person's welfare. The ruler is permitted to regulate the permissible for the public good, and the jurists have used that principle to support a minimum age.

Where child marriage persists, the causes are poverty, weak enforcement and custom, and it exists in non-Muslim societies as well. Reform has often come from within Muslim legal institutions. The point of the laws above is that Muslim scholars and legislators have judged a minimum age to fit the faith, and the countries named are themselves Muslim-majority.

Reform has continued. Indonesia, the country with the largest Muslim population, raised the minimum age of marriage for women from sixteen to nineteen in 2019, the same as for men.[13] The Pakistani province of Sindh set eighteen as the minimum for both sexes in 2013. In each case Muslim scholars and parliaments debated the question in religious terms, and the reformers argued from the welfare of the child, which the jurists placed among the purposes of the law.

The global picture shows that child marriage is not a Muslim problem in particular. UNICEF's figures place the highest rates in parts of West and Central Africa and South Asia, in countries with Muslim, Christian and Hindu majorities, and they link the practice everywhere with poverty, conflict and lack of schooling for girls.[14] Religious arguments are used to defend it in many traditions, and religious leaders in many traditions have worked to end it.

The bottom line

The Quran sets no number but ties marriage to maturity, sound judgement and a solemn covenant. The Prophet made the bride's consent a condition. The classical jurists disagreed about marriage before maturity, and none of them held that a child could be wed and the marriage consummated before she was able.

The reports about Aisha are real and the sources record them, and scholars read them as a particular case. The law is in the commands. Muslim-majority states that set a minimum age of 18 have done so with the support of Muslim jurists. Where child marriage continues, poverty and custom explain it better than scripture does, and defending it with religion goes beyond what the sources require.

A Muslim who wants to protect children has the sources on their side. The Quran's test of sound judgement, the Prophet's insistence on consent, the jurists' rule against harm and the dissent of Ibn Shubruma together give a strong religious case for a minimum age, and Muslim legislators have made that case in their own terms.

  5. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage; Abu Dawud, Book of Marriage. Sunan Abi Dawud 2096 (Book of Marriage), report of Ibn Abbas, graded sahih by al-Albani, checked on sunnah.com.
  6. Ismail Raji al Faruqi, Islam: Religion, Practice, Culture and World Order (London and Washington: The International Institute of Islamic Thought, 2012), p. 61.
  7. Sahih al-Bukhari 5138, Book of Marriage, report of Khansa bint Khidham.
  8. Reported in the books of comparative law, for example Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari, on the chapter of marrying a minor.
  9. Quran 65:4.
  10. Al-Sarakhsi, al-Mabsut, Book of Marriage, on the marriage of minors.
  11. Al-Nawawi, al-Minhaj Sharh Sahih Muslim, commentary on Sahih Muslim 1422, Book of Marriage.
  12. Sahih al-Bukhari, Book of Marriage.
  13. Law of the Republic of Indonesia No. 16 of 2019, amending the Marriage Law No. 1 of 1974.
